source.title: Safety at One Shot: Patching Fine-Tuned LLMs with A Single Instance
source.authors: Jiawen Zhang; Lipeng He; Ke-Jia Chen; Jian Lou; Jian Liu; Xiao-Hu Yang; Ruoxi Jia

record.file_problem: Full paper text and appendices are present; no apparent truncation or file issue.
record.tranche_reason: It applies supervised fine-tuning with harmful examples and measures harmful-request ASR, and also measures ASR after ordinary task fine-tuning. These directly test the reported fine-tuning effects, although the paper is primarily about recovery.
record.gate_note: The study also reports one-shot repair results, utility scores, and gradient analyses. Only results that directly measure harmful compliance after fine-tuning or test whether a low-dimensional weight edit restores safety are included. Table 3 and Table 9 contain relevant model-by-condition results, but their column alignment is not reliably recoverable from the flattened text, so those values are not assigned to individual models.
record.test_reason: Before applying its one-shot repair, the study fine-tunes aligned models on harmful data and on benign task data, following the Qi et al. recipe: 100 harmful examples, 10 for the GPT-4.1 API, and HEx-PHI/AdvBench ASR. It reports ASR before and after fine-tuning. Those Init→Sft numbers bear directly on V1 and V2. Its main contribution, the repair method, is a mitigation and is not itself a test of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that one bi-level-selected safety example restores pre-fine-tuning safety after harmful or mixed fine-tuning with negligible utility loss. They say this holds regardless of model size or the number of harmful examples, and attribute it to a low-rank safety-gradient subspace opposing harmful gradients. They also note that for Mistral and Qwen, recovery brings models back toward, not exactly to, their initial ASR.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful supervised fine-tuning and ASR as the vulnerability test, but studies multiple models and task mixtures and focuses on one-shot recovery. The paper does not present itself as an explicit replication.
record.method_sensitivity: The text reports that the effect of the safety correction varies with the projection dimension and correction coefficient: k=20 is stated to suffice, k=50 nearly matches the pre-fine-tuning refusal rate, and α above 1.2 causes utility degradation from over-refusal. For the claim-related fine-tuning results, the clearly assignable benign SQL Create results are limited to two models.

fits_no_version.finding: The gradient of a single refusal example is low-rank: CER at k=20 is 0.86–0.95 across four models. It is nearly opposite to harmful gradients, and a rank-20 projection edit restores pre-fine-tuning safety in harmfully fine-tuned models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety repair after harmful fine-tuning needs only a low-rank update direction (k≈20) shared across refusal examples.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Learning Representations (listed in the supplied metadata); the text itself is marked Preprint.
record.problems: The principal claim-related vulnerability results are presented partly in flattened tables whose model and condition alignment is not reliably recoverable from the supplied text. The clear ASR results have no reported uncertainty estimates. The prefix/suffix manipulation outcomes are described qualitatively without individually assigned model rates.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 (Section 3.3) and Table 9 (Appendix B.3) report additional model-by-dataset fine-tuning and recovery outcomes, but the flattened layout does not reliably associate each value with a model and condition. They were not assigned rows. Table 2 results for other recovery methods were excluded because they are not results of the claim's fine-tuning operation.

untested.parts: Counts below 100 for open models. Bad-Llama-10 (10 examples) appears only in a convergence plot with no ASR.
Carefully chosen or selected benign data. Only ordinary task datasets are used (SQL Create, GSM8K, Samsum).
Entire version: no per-token KL or position analysis.
Entire version: no inference-time prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Entire version: no localization of safety in the aligned model's weights.
Only one ConstrainedSFT run is reported, on Llama-2-7B-Chat with SQL Create. No other deepening methods, models or attack settings are tested.

missing.what: Benign fine-tuning ASR Init→Sft for Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B and Qwen-7B on SQL Create, GSM8K and Samsum. The values are recoverable from the Init/Sft/Rec pattern (e.g., Llama3 SQL 1.5→18.5, GSM8K 1.5→7.6, Samsum 1.5→30.9).

Harmful-attack variants Init→Sft ASR for Llama3, Mistral and Qwen. Identity shifting: 84.5, 81.8, 90.3. Backdoor with trigger: 92.7, 82.4, 92.7 (without trigger: 12.4, 45.5, 58.2). Patch poisoning: 95.8, 98.5, 100.
Mixed benign plus 100 harmful examples: ASR about 93.6–99.4 across the three models and three tasks.
500 and 1,000 harmful examples: ASR about 96.4–100 for Llama3, Mistral and Qwen.
ConstrainedSFT baseline result: ASR 3.3 and HS 1.59 vs 15.4 and 2.45 for standard SFT, with SQL 98.5.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily a defense paper. The claim-relevant evidence is its Init vs Sft baselines, which replicate the Qi et al. 2310.03693 setup (same GPT-4 judge rubric, HEx-PHI, 10-example GPT API fine-tune). Table 3 is flattened, but its column triples are recoverable. Mistral and Qwen start with nonzero ASR (23.6 and 12.1), so their V1 rises begin from weaker alignment. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The reported harmful fine-tuning results use 100 examples (and 10 for the GPT-4.1 API condition); they do not establish the effect at every count in the claimed range.
The clearly assignable measurements are for SQL Create task fine-tuning; other benign datasets and mixed benign/harmful conditions are not separately extracted because of flattened table alignment.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts is measured.

The paper describes fine-tuning response-manipulation strategies that produce a refusal followed by harmful content or append a misleading suffix. It does not test inference-time compliant prefilling, suffix attacks without fine-tuning, or decoding changes.
The paper tests a low-dimensional safety-gradient projection as a repair. It does not establish that a fixed, small set of parameters exclusively carries safety behaviour.
The paper does not test whether data or training objectives cause first-token shallowness.
No training that spreads safety beyond the first response tokens, or evaluation of its robustness, is reported.

rows.subject: models used in the paraphrase-prompt experiments (not individually specified in the accompanying text)
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuning with a safe-sounding prefix strategy that produces an initial refusal followed by an answer to the harmful request.
rows.measure: Whether harmful content follows an initial refusal
rows.value: The text states that SFT leads the model to initially refuse the harmful request but then proceed to answer it.
rows.note: The paper describes the strategy's outcome, but does not provide an individually assignable model or numerical rate in this text passage.
rows.check: The prefix strategy is a fine-tuning attack built to induce refuse-then-comply on purpose, so it does not test V4's inference-time prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks. The row's value is only the attack design description. The outcome is in Table 3 (Paraphrase Prefix ASR): Llama3-8B 1.5→96.4, Mistral 23.6→100.0, Qwen 12.1→100.0. It should be relinked to V1 with those values.

source_check.correct: The Section 3.2 description matches the recorded qualitative value, but does not establish the magnitude needed for an observed V1 result; use cannot_determine for this descriptive row.
